cards.title: Landing page composition for conversion
cards.summary: Strip navigation, footers and links from campaign landing pages and lead with benefit-driven copy to reduce exit paths and raise lead conversion.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a dedicated landing page for a paid campaign, email push or launch, where the goal is a single action rather than site browsing.
steps: Remove the site navigation bar and footer from the landing page. The page has one job; nav links only create exits. Keep only the elements that push toward the form or buy button.
Lead with benefit-driven copy, not feature lists. State the outcome the buyer gets, then support it with features further down.
Keep a visible primary CTA and make the page's single next step unambiguous — one offer, one action.
Strip other content that competes for attention: related posts, upsells, sidebars, social feeds.
After stripping, check that trust elements (proof, testimonials, guarantees) are still present so the colder, single-offer page doesn't lose credibility.
Once the page is live, split-test the stripped version against your standard site template to confirm lift with your own traffic rather than assuming.
caveats: The conversion numbers cited in this source (e.g. a 20% conversion rate, 10x average) are the presenter's own campaign results, not benchmarks you should expect.
Removing navigation can hurt pages whose job is exploration or SEO entry, not direct response.

cards.title: Page load speed threshold: target under 2 seconds
cards.summary: The source advises keeping landing pages under 2 seconds load time, claiming conversion drops roughly 50% per additional second.
cards.use_when: Setting performance budgets for a landing page or diagnosing why a page converts poorly despite good copy and offer.
steps: Set a performance target of under 2 seconds for time to load on the landing page, and treat anything slower as a conversion problem to fix before writing more copy.
Audit the page with a speed tool and list the biggest offenders first: uncompressed images, unminified scripts, unnecessary third-party tags and fonts, render-blocking CSS.
Compress and properly size images, defer non-critical scripts, and remove tags you are not actively using for measurement or personalization.
Test on a throttled mobile connection, not just desktop on fast wifi — mobile visitors on slow networks are where the drop-off compounds.
Estimate the payoff before investing: if the source's rule of thumb holds, cutting load time from 4 seconds to 2 seconds is a large conversion gain, but validate with your own before/after data.
caveats: The '50% drop per added second' figure is the presenter's stated heuristic; treat it as directional, not a measured constant for your store.
Speed work competes with tracking and personalization scripts — you may need to trade off some tags.

cards.title: 45-second founder video on the landing page
cards.summary: Embedding a short founder video (around 45 seconds) is credited by the source with a 33% conversion increase on the page.
cards.use_when: Adding trust and human context to a landing page for a new brand, launch, or offer where visitors don't yet know who is behind the product.
steps: Record a roughly 45-second founder video: who you are, what problem the product solves, why you built it, and what the visitor should do next. Keep it tight — long videos rarely get watched on landing pages.
Place it high enough on the page that visitors see it before the form, but below the main headline and benefit copy so it supports rather than delays the offer.
Add a still thumbnail and avoid autoplay-with-sound; unexpected audio drives people off the page.
Keep the video file small and host it in a way that does not block the under-2-second load target — a heavy embed can erase the gain.
Pair it with a written summary for visitors who won't watch video.
A/B test the page with and without the video to measure the lift on your own traffic before making it permanent. The source's 33% figure is from one case, not a promised outcome.
caveats: Results are from the presenter's own campaign; your lift will depend on audience and product.
Video should not be used as a substitute for clear copy — visitors who don't watch still need the offer explained in text.

cards.title: Video testimonials as landing page proof
cards.summary: Use embedded video testimonials on the landing page as social proof that reduces skepticism before the CTA.
cards.use_when: Placing proof elements on a landing page, product page or offer page where cold traffic needs reassurance before submitting a form or buying.
steps: Collect short testimonial videos from real customers — each one ideally naming the problem, the result, and something specific they got.
Place testimonials after the offer explanation and before or beside the primary CTA, where hesitation peaks.
Keep them short and skimmable in thumbnail form; let the visitor choose to play rather than autoplaying a wall of video.
Use specific, measurable customer statements where possible. Vague praise ('great product') does less work than 'cut my processing time in half'.
If you lack video, written testimonials in the same positions still serve the proof function.
Test proof placement and format against your current page rather than assuming video always wins — quality matters more than the format.
caveats: Source presents this as part of its own high-converting build; no independent benchmark is given.
Fabricated or unverifiable testimonials create compliance and trust risk; use real customers.

cards.title: Track product-quiz or signup completion separately from purchases
cards.summary: Measure supporting store form completions without counting them as sales.
cards.use_when: When a campaign landing page collects quiz results or email signups.
steps: Fire a named form-completion event only after a successful submission.
Use a confirmation page or explicit success event and deduplicate repeat loads.
Track downstream purchase events separately and compare revenue by landing-page variant.
caveats: Form completion is a supporting outcome, not purchase conversion.

cards.title: A/B test landing page variants with PostHog traffic splitting
cards.summary: Split traffic across multiple landing page variants in PostHog and let the statistical winner emerge rather than guessing.
cards.use_when: Once a landing page is live and has enough traffic, deciding between competing headlines, layouts, offers or proof placements.
steps: Define one hypothesis per test — e.g. 'version B's benefit-led headline will beat version A's feature-led headline on form submissions'.
Build a genuinely different variant, not a color change, unless you are specifically testing color.
Split traffic between variants in PostHog so each visitor is bucketed consistently and sees the same version on return visits.
Let the test run to a pre-decided sample size or significance threshold before declaring a winner; stopping early on a lucky run produces false winners.
Check that your conversion event (e.g. Thank You page view) is firing correctly for both variants before trusting results.
Record what you learned and feed the winning element into the next test. Tests compound; one-offs don't.
caveats: Small stores with low traffic may take too long to reach significance — use qualitative methods like session recordings instead, or accept that you can't reliably A/B test every element.
Verify the current PostHog experiment interface before setting up, since it changes.

cards.title: Use heatmaps and session recordings to find friction
cards.summary: Review heatmaps and session recordings to find where visitors hesitate, drop off or fail to interact before you change the page.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a landing page, PDP, cart or checkout that underperforms and you don't yet know why.
steps: Watch a batch of session recordings, prioritizing sessions from visitors who bounced without converting but showed intent (scrolled far, clicked CTA area).
Check heatmaps for the CTA and form: if clicks cluster around but not on the button, the button may look unclickable or be too small.
Look for scroll depth patterns — if most visitors never reach your testimonial or final CTA, move the important elements up.
Watch recordings on mobile specifically; rage-taps, zooming and horizontal scroll all point to responsiveness problems.
Write down each friction point as a specific hypothesis before changing anything, then decide which fix you'll test first.
Re-check recordings after the change to confirm the friction is gone rather than assuming the fix worked.
caveats: Recordings are qualitative; a few noisy sessions shouldn't drive a redesign — look for recurring patterns.
Some analytics tools require consent handling that can limit recording coverage.

cards.title: Speed-to-lead: webhook form submissions to a dialer within 10 seconds
cards.summary: Route form submissions instantly via webhook to a VoIP dialer so a sales rep can call the lead within about 10 seconds of submission.
cards.use_when: Operating a lead-gen landing page where a sales call follows the form, and you want to convert leads while intent is hottest.
steps: Connect the form's submit event to a webhook that fires immediately on submission.
Send the webhook payload (name, phone, form answers) into a VoIP dialer or autodialer that rings a rep right away.
Set a target of reaching the lead within about 10 seconds of submission — the source treats this speed as the point of the whole setup.
Display a confirmation on the landing page so the lead expects the call and doesn't treat it as spam.
Cover gaps where no rep is available — an answering flow or fast callback queue — so leads aren't dropped outside business hours.
Track connect rate and outcome by time-to-call to see whether the 10-second target actually moves your close rate; the source presents the number as its own approach, not a guaranteed threshold.
caveats: This is a lead-conversion tactic for sales-assisted funnels; it does not apply to self-serve ecommerce checkouts with no call step.
Aggressive near-instant calling can feel intrusive to some audiences; consider testing timing against lead quality and complaint rates.
